title: Railroad day job and parades and funerals in the country
summary: He worked for the Southern Pacific from age 17 until 1921; few parades, and a makeshift funeral band for two burials.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: Did you have, you said you had a day job too, you'd work in the daytime too?
Yeah, I used to work on the railroad.
That'd be the SB, was that?
Southern Pacific. I'd wait there long enough that I had an annual pass. Oh, cool. Yeah, I started waking on the railroad when I was about 17 years old.
I'd wait down there until I came down here in 21. I'm 21.
I was gonna ask you, when you were making out on your trombone, did you never play, you never played a parade with it then, did you?

No, you see, very soon they had parades out there. Yeah. And after carnival, we'd have them floats for carnival, well, they hadn't much news for parades. Sometimes we'd have a little parade. Well, I played a couple of parades, alright, but, like for the old fellas, they may give something, we have a parade. I played a couple of their parades on the land.
Did they ever use any music for funerals there too, when they buried their members of the ensemble?

Let's see. I just could remember they had two funerals. A boy by the name of Henry Jewel, where his daddy used to play bass in the brass band. And I know a young fella, me and him come up together, because he used to stay down there by the name of Joe Camo. He was pretty good trombone, he was playing trombone. Well, when he died, they brought us a boy out in the country, well, we made up a little brand and played in suits. That's about the only one that went out, all our equipment.
